title: Jude and the Undertow
premise: Mirabel Fairweather, a translator whose childhood language is dissolving word by word, is summoned by Emeric Voss, the last fluent speaker, to become his final student before the coastal village of Undertow is demolished for a harbor development. As lessons deepen, Mirabel uncovers photographs implicating his own late father in a decades-old betrayal that sent an innocent man, Tomas Reyes, to prison and scattered the village's speakers. Torn between loyalty to his father's memory and the truth Emeric guards, Mirabel must choose whether to expose the injustice and halt the demolition through testimony rather than law. In the end, he forgives the stranger in the photographs—his father—by speaking the truth aloud in a dying tongue at the public inquiry, saving the village's records if not its walls.
about_author: Freya Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade documenting endangered languages along neglected coastlines. Jude and the Undertow is her second novel, drawn from interviews with the last speakers of three unrecorded dialects.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In a gray city office, Mirabel translates contracts and deflects every personal question with his practiced smile, hiding that he can no longer recall his mother's lullabies. A letter arrives from a village called Undertow. Emotional beat: numbness cracked by a single word he still understands.

chapters.title: A Letter in a Dying Tongue
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The letter, written by one Emeric Voss, requests 'one final student' before spring demolition. Mirabel deciphers half of it, ashamed, and tells himself he won't go. He packs anyway. Emotional beat: reluctant hope wrestling with self-erasure.

chapters.title: Undertow at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He arrives in the condemned village: boarded cafés, surveyor stakes, a sea that sounds like it's chewing the shore. Emeric, sharp-tongued and ancient, tests him with words Mirabel half-remembers. Emotional beat: recognition and grief arriving together.

chapters.title: First Lessons, First Failures
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: Emeric's chapters appear between Mirabel's. Emeric judges Mirabel's accent 'a tourist wearing a native's coat.' Lessons are brutal; Mirabel storms out but returns. Emotional beat: humiliation as the price of belonging.

chapters.title: The House on Rope Walk
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Lodged above the empty fish market, Mirabel finds a box left by the previous tenant: old photographs of village men, including one unmistakably his father, young and laughing beside a man he doesn't recognize. Emotional beat: curiosity shading into unease.

chapters.title: Emeric's Ledger
chapters.summary: Emeric's POV. Emeric has kept a ledger of every word lost, every speaker buried, every promise broken—including one entry dated thirty years ago involving a fire, a trial, and a name crossed out twice. Emotional beat: guilt kept warm like a coal.

chapters.title: Tomas Reyes, Absent
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Villagers mention Tomas Reyes only in past tense though no one says he died. Mirabel learns Tomas was convicted of arson that destroyed the language school—the reason so few speakers remain. His father testified against him. Emotional beat: the floor tilting under family myth.

chapters.title: Words for Things That No Longer Exist
chapters.summary: Emeric's POV. Teaching resumes; Emeric introduces words with no living referents—a boat type, a tide-wind, a greeting between brothers. He watches Mirabel absorb them and wonders if truth can be taught like vocabulary. Emotional beat: tenderness disguised as rigor.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel confronts Emeric with the photos. Emeric confirms: his father and Tomas were closest friends until the fire. 'Your father lied,' Emeric says, 'and I let him.' Emotional beat: betrayal compounding betrayal; loyalty beginning to rot.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Defending his dead father, Mirabel nearly quits, drafting a furious letter home he never sends. He walks the demolition perimeter and realizes anger is easier than grief. Emotional beat: defensive loyalty cracking into doubt.

chapters.title: The Night of the Fire, Retold
chapters.summary: Emeric's POV. Emeric recounts the true night: the school burned to destroy debt records implicating developers; Tomas took the blame after Mirabel's father, coerced and terrified, gave false testimony. Emeric stayed silent to protect his own family. Emotional beat: confession as slow bleeding.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Official notices appear: bulldozers in six weeks. Villagers split between resignation and a last-ditch heritage petition that needs 'substantive cultural testimony'—a hearing, not a courtroom. Emotional beat: deadline pressure turning private history public.

chapters.title: Learning to Speak Again
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel throws himself into lessons, discovering fluency isn't memory returning but something built new. He dreams in the old tongue for the first time since childhood. Emotional beat: quiet joy, the book's first real warmth.

chapters.title: The Petition
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, mostly Mirabel's POV. Villagers gather testimonies; some refuse to speak of Tomas, others weep at his name. Mirabel realizes his father's lie is the keystone holding everyone's silence up. Emotional beat: collective fear of truth.

chapters.title: A Visit from the Developer's Man
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A smooth company liaison offers Mirabel money to translate the village's land deeds 'accurately'—meaning favorably—and hints the hearing is theater. Mirabel declines badly, shaken. Emotional beat: temptation and the taste of complicity.

chapters.title: Emeric Falters
chapters.summary: Emeric's POV. Emeric suffers a small stroke; his speech slips, words falling away even as he teaches. He begs Mirabel to memorize faster, then confesses he may not live to testify himself. Emotional beat: urgency sharpened into love.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At his father's grave-equivalent—an unmarked bench—he speaks aloud, in the old language, everything he now knows, and finds the anger dissolving into sorrow. Forgiveness arrives not as absolution but as understanding. Emotional beat: the thematic heart; release.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Before the inquiry, Mirabel testifies—not about land value but about the fire, naming his father's perjury and Tomas's innocence, in both languages, while Emeric corroborates from a wheelchair. The room fractures. Emotional beat: climax; truth spoken at personal cost.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Truth
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The verdict: demolition proceeds, but the village wins protected status for its archive and a memorial site; Tomas's case is reopened posthumously. Some villagers thank Mirabel; others turn away. Emotional beat: justice outside the law is partial, and real.

chapters.title: Tomas Comes Home
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Tomas Reyes, alive, elderly, exiled these thirty years, returns for the exoneration. He and Emeric speak a greeting between brothers that exists in no dictionary. Mirabel translates nothing; some things need no translation. Emotional beat: reconciliation earned.

chapters.title: The Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Emeric's POV. On the final morning before the walls come down, Emeric gives Mirabel his last lesson: not vocabulary but the blessing mothers said over departing boats. He names Mirabel a speaker, not a student. Emotional beat: transmission complete; elegy and gift.

chapters.title: Jude and the Undertow
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Months later, Mirabel teaches the language to children in a rented hall, keeping the archive alive as the village becomes memory. He has stopped perfecting the smile that ends conversations; he uses the one that starts them. Emotional beat: resolution—language survives its speakers when someone chooses to carry it.
